claims.claim: Flies prefer 0.5% agarose with sugar over 2.0% agarose with sugar during feeding.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that flies generally prefer the softer of two sweet substrates during feeding; for example, they prefer 0.5% agarose with sugar over 2.0% agarose with sugar (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This specific preference is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Feeding preference for softer substrates requires inputs from at least two distinct groups of mechanosensitive neurons on the labellum.
claims.source: This feeding preference requires inputs from at least two distinct groups of mechanosensitive neurons on the labellum: one that uses the evolutionarily conserved mechanosensitive channel Transmembrane Channel-like (TMC) to sense hardness of substrates during discrimination of substrates, whereas the other uses the TRP channels NompC and Nanchung (Nan) (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This claim about the neural basis of feeding preference is supported by citations.

claims.claim: One group of mechanosensitive neurons uses TMC to sense hardness of substrates during discrimination.
claims.source: This feeding preference requires inputs from at least two distinct groups of mechanosensitive neurons on the labellum: one that uses the evolutionarily conserved mechanosensitive channel Transmembrane Channel-like (TMC) to sense hardness of substrates during discrimination of substrates, whereas the other uses the TRP channels NompC and Nanchung (Nan) (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Another group of mechanosensitive neurons uses the TRP channels NompC and Nanchung (Nan).
claims.source: This feeding preference requires inputs from at least two distinct groups of mechanosensitive neurons on the labellum: one that uses the evolutionarily conserved mechanosensitive channel Transmembrane Channel-like (TMC) to sense hardness of substrates during discrimination of substrates, whereas the other uses the TRP channels NompC and Nanchung (Nan) (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Activation of NompC/Nan-expressing neurons can directly inhibit the output of sweet-sensing taste neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, activation of the group that expressed NompC and Nan channels can directly inhibit the output of the sweet-sensing taste neurons, thereby further increasing the 'food value' of the softer substrate – the harder substrate should taste less sweet than the softer one because it induces stronger activation of the NompC/Nan-expressing neurons (that then exerts stronger suppression of output of sweet neurons) (Jeong et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This mechanism is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Flies laid comparable numbers of eggs on agarose whose concentration ranged from 0.25% to 1.5% in single-choice assays.
claims.source: We found that flies laid comparable numbers of eggs on agarose whose concentration ranged from 0.25% to 1.5% (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in the data presented in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Flies laid fewer eggs on agarose with concentrations that were either too high or too low.
claims.source: But they laid fewer eggs on agarose with concentrations that were either too high or too low (Figure 1B), likely because they cannot easily insert their ovipositor into a substrate that is very hard and because they tend to avoid walking on a surface that is liquid-like.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and explained with inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Flies consistently laid more eggs on 0.5% agarose when it was pitted against 1.0%, 1.25% or 1.5% agarose in two-choice assays.
claims.source: We found that flies consistently laid more eggs on the 0.5% agarose when it was pitted against 1.0%, 1.25% or 1.5% agarose in different two-choice assays (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in the data presented in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Flies are capable of discriminating 'equally acceptable' substrates of different hardness.
claims.source: Since flies laid comparable amount of eggs on these concentrations of agarose in single-choice assays (Figure 1B), their preference for the softer 0.5% agarose in the two-choice assays indicated that: 1) they were capable of discriminating 'equally acceptable' substrates of different hardness and 2) they preferred the softer one when given a choice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing single-choice and two-choice assay results.

claims.claim: Flies preferred the softer substrate when given a choice between equally acceptable substrates of different hardness.
claims.source: Since flies laid comparable amount of eggs on these concentrations of agarose in single-choice assays (Figure 1B), their preference for the softer 0.5% agarose in the two-choice assays indicated that: 1) they were capable of discriminating 'equally acceptable' substrates of different hardness and 2) they preferred the softer one when given a choice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing single-choice and two-choice assay results.

claims.claim: Flies spent comparable amounts of time on 0.5% and 1.5% agarose substrates in two-choice assays.
claims.source: Further, tracking the positions of flies as they explored and laid eggs in a 0.5% vs. 1.5% two-choice assay showed that they spent comparable amounts of time on these two agarose substrates (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that their preference to deposit eggs on the softer 0.5% agarose substrate was not due to intrinsic positional preference for the softer substrate.
claims.evidence: This is shown by tracking data in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: Flies' preference to deposit eggs on the softer substrate was not due to intrinsic positional preference for the softer substrate.
claims.source: Further, tracking the positions of flies as they explored and laid eggs in a 0.5% vs. 1.5% two-choice assay showed that they spent comparable amounts of time on these two agarose substrates (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that their preference to deposit eggs on the softer 0.5% agarose substrate was not due to intrinsic positional preference for the softer substrate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the tracking data showing equal time spent on both substrates.

claims.claim: Mutants for ppk28, Nan, Iav, NompC, Piezo, and TMC all showed a preference to deposit eggs on the softer 0.5% agarose substrate when given a choice between 0.5% and 1.5% agarose.
claims.source: Curiously, none of these mutants behaved differently from controls: they all showed a preference to deposit their eggs on the softer 0.5% agarose substrate when given a 0.5% and a 1.5% agarose substrate to choose from (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Silencing TMC-expressing neurons did not significantly impact flies' ability to discriminate substrates of different hardness during egg-laying.
claims.source: However, silencing these neurons by using the same tools employed by the feeding studies (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b) did not significantly impact flies' ability to discriminate substrates of different hardness during egg-laying either: these manipulated flies still clearly preferred to lay eggs on the 0.5% agarose in the 0.5% vs. 1.5% two-choice assays (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: Silencing NompC and Nan-expressing neurons did not significantly impact flies' ability to discriminate substrates of different hardness during egg-laying.
claims.source: However, silencing these neurons by using the same tools employed by the feeding studies (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b) did not significantly impact flies' ability to discriminate substrates of different hardness during egg-laying either: these manipulated flies still clearly preferred to lay eggs on the 0.5% agarose in the 0.5% vs. 1.5% two-choice assays (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: Removing the ovipositor caused animals unable to lay any eggs.
claims.source: We severed different appendages one at a time and found that, first, not surprisingly, removing the ovipositor caused animals unable to lay any eggs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Severing the labellum, tarsi, or both did not cause any reduction in substrate hardness discrimination during egg-laying.
claims.source: However interestingly, we found that severing the rest of the appendages either singly or together did not cause any reduction in substrate hardness discrimination during egg-laying (Figure 2E–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 2E-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Flies without labellum or tarsi from all six legs showed significantly stronger preference for the softer substrate than controls.
claims.source: More strikingly, flies without labellum or tarsi from all six legs – or both – not only still showed a clear preference to lay eggs on the softer of two substrates, their preference for the softer substrate was significantly stronger than controls (Figure 2E–G), suggesting that these appendages may house mechanosensitive neurons that can act to inhibit hardness discrimination during egg-laying.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 2E-G.

claims.claim: Labellum and tarsi may house mechanosensitive neurons that can act to inhibit hardness discrimination during egg-laying.
claims.source: More strikingly, flies without labellum or tarsi from all six legs – or both – not only still showed a clear preference to lay eggs on the softer of two substrates, their preference for the softer substrate was significantly stronger than controls (Figure 2E–G), suggesting that these appendages may house mechanosensitive neurons that can act to inhibit hardness discrimination during egg-laying.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced discrimination observed when these appendages are removed.

claims.claim: Flies use different sets of mechanosensitive channels to discriminate substrates of different hardness during feeding and egg-laying.
claims.source: First, flies use different sets of mechanosensitive channels to discriminate substrates of different hardness during feeding and egg-laying – TMC, NompC, and Nan were not required for discrimination during egg-laying (Figure 2A) but were required for discrimination during feeding (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from comparing the current results with previous feeding studies.

claims.claim: TMC, NompC, and Nan were not required for discrimination during egg-laying.
claims.source: First, flies use different sets of mechanosensitive channels to discriminate substrates of different hardness during feeding and egg-laying – TMC, NompC, and Nan were not required for discrimination during egg-laying (Figure 2A) but were required for discrimination during feeding (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: TMC, NompC, and Nan were required for discrimination during feeding.
claims.source: First, flies use different sets of mechanosensitive channels to discriminate substrates of different hardness during feeding and egg-laying – TMC, NompC, and Nan were not required for discrimination during egg-laying (Figure 2A) but were required for discrimination during feeding (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous feeding studies.

claims.claim: The principal mechanosensitive neurons flies use to discriminate hardness during egg-laying likely may be housed on the ovipositor.
claims.source: Second, although flies rely on mechanosensitive neurons on the labellum/proboscis to discriminate substrates of different hardness during feeding (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2017b), the principal mechanosensitive neurons they use to discriminate hardness during egg-laying likely may be housed on the ovipositor instead since removal of none of the other appendages caused females unable to discriminate substrates of different hardness (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the appendage removal experiments.

claims.claim: Ovipositor is known to possess mechanosensitive neurons.
claims.source: We based this tentative model on the following reasons. First, ovipositor is known to possess mechanosensitive neurons (Sánchez-Alcañiz and Benton, 2017a; Stocker, 1994; Newland and Burrows, 1994); second, flies have been shown to actively probe the substrates with their ovipositor prior to depositing each egg (Yang et al., 2008); third and most importantly, animals that lacked the a significant portion of virtually all other appendages (e.g. labellum, tarsi, wings) but had intact ovipositor were still capable of discriminating substrates of different hardness.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Flies have been shown to actively probe the substrates with their ovipositor prior to depositing each egg.
claims.source: We based this tentative model on the following reasons. First, ovipositor is known to possess mechanosensitive neurons (Sánchez-Alcañiz and Benton, 2017a; Stocker, 1994; Newland and Burrows, 1994); second, flies have been shown to actively probe the substrates with their ovipositor prior to depositing each egg (Yang et al., 2008); third and most importantly, animals that lacked the a significant portion of virtually all other appendages (e.g. labellum, tarsi, wings) but had intact ovipositor were still capable of discriminating substrates of different hardness.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous behavioral study.

claims.claim: Presence of sucrose in both substrates significantly reduced females' preference to lay eggs on the softer 0.5% substrate.
claims.source: Specifically, we added the same amount of sucrose to both the 0.5% and the 1.5% agarose substrates and found that, interestingly, presence of sucrose in both substrates significantly reduced females' preference to lay eggs on the softer 0.5% substrate (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: The reduction in preference for softer substrate was mild when sucrose concentration was low (e.g. 5 mM) but became stronger as the concentration of sucrose increased.
claims.source: The reduction in preference was mild when sucrose concentration was low (e.g. 5 mM) but became stronger as the concentration of sucrose increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: When sucrose concentration reached 100 mM, flies became virtually indifferent between the 0.5% and the 1.5% choice.
claims.source: When the concentration reached 100 mM, flies became virtually indifferent between the 0.5% and the 1.5% choice (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: A similar reduction in discrimination was observed when sucrose was replaced with several other sweet compounds or pineapple juice.
claims.source: A similar reduction in discrimination was observed when sucrose was replaced with several other sweet compounds, pineapple juice, but not with sorbitol, which is a nutritious but unsweet substance for flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Sorbitol, which is a nutritious but unsweet substance for flies, did not reduce discrimination of substrates of different hardness.
claims.source: A similar reduction in discrimination was observed when sucrose was replaced with several other sweet compounds, pineapple juice, but not with sorbitol, which is a nutritious but unsweet substance for flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Presence of the bitter chemical caffeine or the sour chemical acetic acid did not significantly impact discrimination of substrates of different hardness.
claims.source: Furthermore, because a previous report has shown that arena size can influence how animals behaviorally respond to sucrose during egg-laying site selection (Schwartz et al., 2012), we also examined whether sucrose was similarly capable of reducing discrimination of substrates of different hardness when animals were selecting for egg-laying substrates in larger arenas.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Flies in arenas that were ~8X the size still preferred the softer 0.5% agarose over the 1.5% agarose when both substrates were sucrose free but reduced their soft preference when both contained 100 mM sucrose.
claims.source: We found that, similar to what we have observed in our 'regular arenas', flies in arenas that were ~8X the size still preferred the softer 0.5% agarose over the 1.5% agarose when both substrates were sucrose free but reduced their soft preference when both contained 100 mM sucrose (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: Presence of sucrose in substrates can cause females to become less discriminating between substrates of different hardness during egg-laying.
claims.source: Together, these results showed that the presence of sweet compounds in substrates can cause females to become less discriminating between substrates of different hardness during egg-laying.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the collective results of the sucrose experiments.

claims.claim: While the presence of different concentrations of sucrose did slightly alter the hardness of both the 0.5% and the 1.5% agarose substrates, differences in hardness between the two substrates remained significantly different.
claims.source: We found that while the presence of different concentrations of sucrose did slightly alter the hardness of both the 0.5% and the 1.5% agarose substrates, differences in hardness between the two substrates remained significantly different (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by the hardness measurements in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Eliminating the tarsi or labellum significantly increased flies' preference for the softer substrate in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: We first severed different appendages that are known to house sweet neurons and found that eliminating the tarsi or labellum significantly increased flies' preference for the softer substrate in the presence of sucrose (Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D-F.

claims.claim: Severing the antennae also increased soft preference in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: Interestingly, while severing neither the wings nor the maxillary palps had any significant effect, severing the antennae also increased soft preference in the presence of sucrose (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claims.claim: Some olfactory neurons express specific molecular sugar receptors and these neurons thus may potentially be capable sensing sugars.
claims.source: (It is worth noting that recent reports have suggested that some olfactory neurons express specific molecular sugar receptors and these neurons thus may potentially be capable sensing sugars, too [Fujii et al., 2015; Yavuz et al., 2014])
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent reports.

claims.claim: Mutants that are known to be defective in sugar sensing showed a clear preference for the softer substrate in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: We next removed several molecular sugar receptors from flies and found that mutants that are known to be defective in sugar sensing (Fujii et al., 2015; Yavuz et al., 2014) also showed a clear preference for the softer substrate in the presence of sucrose (Figure 3G), as did flies with their sweet neurons selectively silenced (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Flies with their sweet neurons selectively silenced showed a clear preference for the softer substrate in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: We next removed several molecular sugar receptors from flies and found that mutants that are known to be defective in sugar sensing (Fujii et al., 2015; Yavuz et al., 2014) also showed a clear preference for the softer substrate in the presence of sucrose (Figure 3G), as did flies with their sweet neurons selectively silenced (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Silencing only the sweet-sensing neurons on the legs but not on the labellum recovered some soft preference.
claims.source: Further, silencing only the sweet-sensing neurons on the legs but not on the labellum (labeled by Gr64aGAL4) (Fujii et al., 2015) recovered some soft preference (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), too, albeit to a lesser extent than silencing all sweet neurons.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Silencing the bitter-sensing taste neurons failed to recover significant soft preference in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: As a control, we also silenced the bitter-sensing taste neurons and found that it failed to recover significant soft preference in the presence of sucrose (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Silencing sweet neurons did not enhance discrimination of substrates of different hardness when the substrates were sugar free.
claims.source: Lastly, we showed that the improvements of hardness discrimination in the presence of sucrose by inhibiting sweet sensing were not because sweet neurons can act as inhibitors of hardness discrimination in general: silencing sweet neurons did not enhance discrimination of substrates of different hardness when the substrates were sugar free (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I.

claims.claim: Presence of sweet compounds on egg-laying substrates of different hardness can cause females to become less discriminating between them and reduce their preference for the softer one.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that presence of sweet compounds on egg-laying substrates of different hardness can cause females to become less discriminating between them and reduce their preference for the softer one.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the collective results of the sucrose and sweet neuron manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Sucrose-induced indifference towards substrates of different hardness requires activation of sweet neurons on flies' labellum, tarsi, and possibly also on antennae.
claims.source: Further, such sucrose-induced indifference towards substrates of different hardness requires activation of sweet neurons on flies' labellum, tarsi, and possibly also on antennae (even though it is presently unclear whether Gr64f-expressing neurons on the antennae are truly capable of sensing sugar).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the appendage removal and genetic manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Several independently generated tmc mutants showed a strong preference for the softer substrate despite the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: Indeed, whereas most of these mutants behaved similarly to controls (Figure 4A), several independently generated tmc mutants (Zhang et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2016) behaved differently from the rest and showed a strong preference for the softer substrate despite the presence of sucrose (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: TMC channel, like sweet neurons, may act to inhibit discrimination of substrates of different hardness in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: These results suggest TMC channel, like sweet neurons, may act to inhibit discrimination of substrates of different hardness in the presence of sucrose.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of tmc mutants in the presence of sucrose.

claims.claim: Reintroducing the tmc gene back to the tmc1 mutants reverted them to behave more like WT animals: they were less discriminating of substrates of different hardness in the presence of sucrose.
claims.source: We found that this manipulation reverted tmc1 mutants to behave more like WT animals: they were less discriminating of substrates of different hardness in the presence of sucrose (Figure 4C).

results.result: Drosophila females discriminate and prefer softer egg-laying substrates in the absence of sucrose. Flies laid comparable numbers of eggs on 0.25-1.5% agarose in single-choice assays but consistently preferred 0.5% over harder substrates (1.0-1.5%) in two-choice assays, despite spending equal time on both substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 provide converging behavioral evidence from single-choice and two-choice assays, supported by tracking data (Figure 1B, D, E, F). The preference is not due to positional bias, as flies spent equal time on both substrates. The data demonstrate both discrimination ability and preference for softer substrates.

results.result: Mechanosensory channels and neurons required for hardness discrimination during feeding are not required for egg-laying substrate discrimination. Mutants for TMC, NompC, Nan, Piezo, and other channels retained normal hardness discrimination during egg-laying. Removal of labellum or tarsi enhanced rather than impaired discrimination, suggesting these appendages house inhibitory mechanosensitive neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C43 are well-supported by genetic mutant analysis (Figure 2A) and surgical ablation experiments (Figure 2E-G). The enhanced discrimination after appendage removal is particularly striking and suggests an inhibitory role. The contrast with feeding behavior (C40-C42) is supported by citations to prior work.

results.result: Presence of sucrose on both substrates reduces discrimination of hardness during egg-laying in a dose-dependent manner. At 100 mM sucrose, flies became indifferent between 0.5% and 1.5% agarose. This effect was specific to sweet compounds and not due to changes in substrate hardness, as physical measurements showed hardness differences remained significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 are strongly supported by behavioral data (Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C) and physical hardness measurements (Figure 3C). The dose-response relationship, specificity to sweet compounds (not sorbitol, caffeine, or acetic acid), and persistence across different arena sizes provide robust evidence.

results.result: Sucrose-induced reduction in hardness discrimination requires functional sweet neurons on labellum, tarsi, and possibly antennae. Surgical removal of these appendages or genetic silencing of sweet neurons restored preference for softer substrates in the presence of sucrose. This effect was specific to sweet neurons, as silencing bitter neurons had no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C64 are supported by surgical ablation (Figure 3D-F), genetic receptor mutants (Figure 3G), and neuronal silencing experiments (Figure 3H-I). Multiple independent approaches converge on the same conclusion. Controls (bitter neurons, sugar-free conditions) strengthen the interpretation.

results.result: TMC channel and TMC-expressing mechanosensitive neurons on the labellum are required for sucrose-induced inhibition of hardness discrimination. Multiple tmc mutants showed strong preference for softer substrates despite sucrose presence. Genetic rescue and cell-specific silencing experiments confirmed the requirement for peripheral TMC neurons on the labellum.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C75 are well-supported by multiple independent tmc mutants (Figure 4A-B), genetic rescue (Figure 4C), neuronal silencing with spatial controls using vGlut-GAL80 (Figure 4D-F), and comparison of different GAL4 drivers (Figure 4G-I). The convergence of genetic and cell-specific manipulations provides strong evidence.

results.result: TMC mutants and flies with silenced TMC neurons retain normal sugar sensing ability, as they discriminate substrates with different sucrose concentrations. This is consistent with prior electrophysiological data showing TMC neurons respond normally to sucrose.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by behavioral discrimination assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F) and citation to prior electrophysiology (C73). This control is important for ruling out the alternative explanation that tmc mutants simply cannot sense sugar.

results.result: Axons of sweet neurons and TMC-expressing neurons physically contact each other in the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the brain. Both conventional GRASP and syb:GRASP techniques detected reconstituted GFP in the SEZ, suggesting sweet neurons may act as presynaptic partners to TMC neuron axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by anatomical data (Figure 5A-B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D) using two independent GRASP techniques. The syb:GRASP result (C79-C80) is particularly informative as it suggests synaptic contact. The absence of signal in ventral nerve cord (C81) provides spatial specificity.

results.result: Sucrose application increases calcium influx into TMC neuron axons in the brain. This response requires functional sweet receptors (Gr64f) and is not observed with sorbitol. TMC neuron cell bodies do not respond to sucrose, and the response is reduced in tmc mutants, suggesting co-activation of sweet neurons and TMC channels is required.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88 are supported by calcium imaging experiments (Figure 5D-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D) with appropriate controls. The specificity for sucrose vs. sorbitol (C83), requirement for Gr64f (C85), lack of response in cell bodies (C84), and reduced response in tmc mutants (C87) provide strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Artificial activation of sweet neurons using P2X2 channels increases calcium influx into TMC neuron axons. ATP stimulation of P2X2-expressing sweet neurons triggered increased GCaMP signal in TMC axons, while control animals without P2X2 showed no response.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by chemogenetic activation experiments (Figure 5F-G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-F). This provides independent confirmation that sweet neuron activation can modulate TMC neuron activity, complementing the sucrose application experiments.

results.result: Drosophila integrate mechanosensory and chemosensory information during egg-laying site selection through a mechanism where sweet neurons directly enhance TMC neuron output. This integration causes flies to switch from preferring softer substrates to being indifferent when both contain sucrose, requiring both functional sweet neurons and TMC-expressing mechanosensitive neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C8, C91-C95 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental results. The integration mechanism is supported by behavioral (preference switch), genetic (requirement for both sweet and TMC neurons), anatomical (axon-axon contacts), and functional (calcium imaging) evidence. This represents a complete demonstration of sensory integration.

results.result: Flies use different sensory mechanisms for hardness discrimination during feeding versus egg-laying. TMC neurons promote discrimination during feeding but inhibit it during egg-laying in the presence of sucrose. The authors propose that unidentified mechanosensitive neurons on the ovipositor mediate hardness discrimination during egg-laying.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 are partially supported. The different roles of TMC neurons in feeding vs. egg-laying are demonstrated (C103-C104, Figure 4—figure supplement 3F). However, the proposal that ovipositor neurons mediate egg-laying discrimination (C105) is speculative, based on indirect evidence (inability to test after ovipositor removal, persistence after other appendage removal). Direct identification of these neurons is needed.

results.result: Tarsi and antennae contribute to sucrose-induced inhibition of hardness discrimination, and tmc transcripts are present on these appendages. However, direct artificial activation of TMC neurons severely reduced egg-laying rate, preventing assessment of sufficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 identify limitations in the current work. While tmc transcripts are detected on tarsi and antennae (C98, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), the functional relationship with sweet neurons on these structures is unclear (C97). The inability to test sufficiency due to behavioral disruption (C99, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-I) represents an important gap.

results.result: The authors propose that mechanosensitive and sweet neurons can have bidirectional interactions: presynaptic inhibition from mechanosensitive to sweet neurons (as shown in prior work) and presynaptic facilitation from sweet to TMC neurons (as shown here).
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 attempt to reconcile current findings with prior literature. While C100-C101 accurately cite prior work, the proposed bidirectional interaction model (C102) is speculative. The model is plausible but lacks direct experimental support in this manuscript. Additional experiments would be needed to demonstrate both types of interactions occur simultaneously.

results.result: The authors speculate that sucrose-induced indifference may be adaptive when substrate differences are small, and that this mechanism could provide evolutionary substrate for species-specific texture selectivity, as seen in Drosophila suzukii.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 are speculative interpretations about adaptive value and evolutionary implications. While C108 is supported by behavioral data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and C110 by citations, the adaptive explanations (C106-C107) and evolutionary hypotheses (C109) are not tested. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work but are not experimentally validated.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about sensory integration, Drosophila egg-laying behavior, and mechanosensory mechanisms during feeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C9-C25 represent background information supported by citations to prior literature. These establish the context and motivation for the current study. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent prior work on sensory integration, egg-laying behavior, and feeding-related mechanosensation.

results.result: Supporting anatomical and molecular facts from prior literature: ovipositor contains mechanosensitive neurons, flies probe substrates with ovipositor, some olfactory neurons express sugar receptors, and Gr64f is important for sugar sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45, C57, C86 cite prior literature to support specific anatomical and molecular facts. These citations appear accurate and provide important context for interpreting the current results. C57 appropriately notes uncertainty about whether antennal neurons truly sense sugar.
